concept.name: Kappa Stream-Only Architecture

relationships.description: Connects Kappa Stream-Only Architecture to data warehousing lakehouse in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Kappa architecture eliminates the separate batch layer of Lambda architecture by treating an append-only distributed log as the single source of truth for both real-time processing and historical replay.
spark.keyTakeaway: One code path, one immutable log: when business logic changes, you spin up a second stream job from offset 0, backfill a new serving table, and atomically swap pointers.

concept.whyItMatters: Lambda architecture forces teams to write, test, and reconcile two completely different codebases—say, Spark SQL for nightly batch corrections and Apache Flink for real-time metrics—guaranteeing subtle semantic drift between yesterday's dashboard and today's.
whenToUse: Real-time analytics, fraud scoring, CDC materialized views, and feature stores where maintaining dual batch/stream codebases causes drift.
Event-sourced domains where retaining days, months, or infinite history in Kafka Tiered Storage (S3/GCS) or Apache Pulsar is practical.
Teams already invested in stateful stream engines (Apache Flink, Kafka Streams) with deterministic event-time processing.
whenNotToUse: Complex multi-table ad-hoc joins, global graph algorithms (PageRank), or ML training over petabytes of cold Parquet data better suited to Spark/Snowflake.
Workloads where raw events cannot be retained in a log long enough to cover full historical reprocessing windows.
Small organizations without operational expertise in RocksDB state backends, Flink checkpointing, or Kafka topic partitioning.
keyPoints: Immutable log as SSOT: Apache Kafka (`log.retention.ms=-1` or Tiered Storage to S3/GCS) stores the canonical, ordered history of events.
Single stream codebase: one Flink or Kafka Streams job handles both live tailing and historical reprocessing using event-time watermarks.
Blue/Green replay workflow: to fix a bug or change a schema, deploy `job-v2` reading from offset 0 into `view_v2`, let it catch up to the live tail, and atomically swap the serving alias.
Stateful stream processing: engines like Flink embed RocksDB for multi-terabyte keyed state with incremental checkpoints to object storage for exactly-once recovery.
Compaction for entity state: Kafka log compaction (`cleanup.policy=compact`) keeps the latest state per key indefinitely without unbounded storage growth.

examples.title: Fixing a Double-Counting Bug via Flink Replay
examples.scenario: A ride-sharing surge-pricing pipeline discovers a bug in `surge-v1` that double-counted cancelled trip events over the past 14 days.
examples.outcome: Engineers deploy `surge-v2` with a new consumer group starting at the 14-day-ago Kafka offset in Tiered Storage. Flink processes 14 days of events at 400k events/sec into a fresh OpenSearch index `surge_v2`, catches up to real-time in 45 minutes, and flips the `surge_live` alias atomically.

examples.title: Unified Feature Store for Fraud Detection
examples.scenario: A payments team previously suffered model skew because offline training features were computed in Spark while online features ran in Storm.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Kappa with Kafka + Flink writes identical event-time windowed aggregations (`tx_count_1h`, `avg_amount_24h`) to both Redis (online serving) and Apache Iceberg (offline training), eliminating training-serving skew.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates maintaining two separate frameworks (Spark batch + Flink stream) and reconciling their outputs.
tradeOffs.con: Replaying 90 days of high-volume events through a stream engine requires temporary autoscaling of Flink TaskManagers and RocksDB IOPS.

tradeOffs.pro: Kafka Tiered Storage offloads old segments to S3/GCS at ~$0.023/GB-month instead of expensive NVMe broker disks.
tradeOffs.con: Reading historical segments from object storage has higher latency and egress/API costs if replayed frequently.

tradeOffs.pro: Watermarks and `AllowedLateness` handle out-of-order mobile events deterministically across both live and replay runs.
tradeOffs.con: Side-effecting external API calls inside a stream job are unsafe during replay unless gated by idempotency keys or suppressed.

failureModes.name: Replay Thundering Herd on Serving DB
failureModes.description: Replaying 30 days of events at 500k events/sec hammers the live PostgreSQL/Redis cluster, starving real-time user queries.
failureModes.mitigation: Write replay output to an isolated staging table/index (`view_v2`), throttle sink writes, or bulk-load SSTables/Iceberg files before swapping.

failureModes.name: Non-Deterministic Processing on Replay
failureModes.description: Stream code calls `System.currentTimeMillis()`, `UUID.randomUUID()`, or queries a mutable external database during enrichment, producing different results on replay.
failureModes.mitigation: Use event-time timestamps from the Kafka record, deterministic IDs, and temporal joins against CDC-streamed dimension tables.

failureModes.name: RocksDB State Explosion
failureModes.description: Unbounded key cardinality without state TTL causes Flink RocksDB checkpoints to grow to terabytes and time out.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure `StateTtlConfig` on keyed state descriptors and enable incremental RocksDB checkpoints.

failureModes.name: Watermark Stall from Idle Partitions
failureModes.description: One quiet Kafka partition receives no events for 10 minutes, freezing the global event-time watermark and stalling all windowed outputs.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure `WatermarkStrategy.withIdleness(Duration.ofSeconds(30))` so active partitions advance the watermark.

commonMistakes: Replaying directly into the live production table (`UPSERT` in place), corrupting active views with mixed v1 and v2 aggregations.
Using processing time (`System.currentTimeMillis()`) instead of event time, which collapses 30 days of historical events into a single 10-minute window during replay.
Keeping infinite retention on raw Kafka NVMe broker disks instead of enabling Tiered Storage or Iceberg/Parquet archival.
Forgetting to handle late-arriving events or tombstones (`null` payloads) in compacted topics.
Triggering external webhooks, emails, or payment charges directly inside a replayable stream topology without idempotency guards.

sections.content:
## The idea

Proposed by Jay Kreps in 2014 as a reaction to the operational pain of Lambda architecture, **Kappa architecture** asks a simple question: *if a stream processor can already handle real-time data and you can retain the input log long enough to reprocess it, why maintain a second batch engine at all?*

In Kappa, an append-only distributed log (Apache Kafka, Redpanda, or Pulsar) is the canonical source of truth. Both real-time serving and historical corrections execute the exact same stream-processing codebase. When you discover a bug or introduce a new metric, you don't write a Spark backfill script—you deploy version 2 of your stream job reading from offset 0 into a parallel output table, wait for it to catch up to the live tail, and atomically switch the application's read pointer.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose `orders-events` (24 partitions, Kafka Tiered Storage in S3) feeds `revenue-agg-v1` in Apache Flink, writing hourly totals to OpenSearch index `revenue_v1` (aliased as `revenue_live`).

1. **Bug Discovery**: A tax-rounding bug is found in `v1` affecting the last 30 days.
2. **Parallel Deploy**: Engineers deploy `revenue-agg-v2` with a fresh consumer group (`group-v2`) configured with `auto.offset.reset=earliest` (or a timestamp offset from 30 days ago) and target index `revenue_v2`.
3. **Catch-Up Replay**: Flink scales to 48 TaskManagers, streams 30 days of historical segments from S3 Tiered Storage using event-time watermarks, and builds `revenue_v2` in 35 minutes without touching `revenue_v1`.
4. **Atomic Swap & Decommission**: Once `group-v2` consumer lag hits ~0 (matching `v1` at the live tail), an atomic OpenSearch `_aliases` swap points `revenue_live` from `revenue_v1` to `revenue_v2`. `revenue-agg-v1` and `revenue_v1` are then safely retired.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Event time, watermarks, and deterministic state
sections.content:
## Event time, watermarks, and deterministic state

For a replay to produce the exact same output as live execution, the stream engine must be strictly **deterministic**:

- **Event Time over Processing Time**: Always window by the timestamp embedded in the event payload (`order.created_at`), never the wall clock of the Flink TaskManager.
- **Watermarks**: A watermark `W(t)` asserts that no more events with timestamp `< t` are expected. During a fast replay, event-time windows close deterministically based on the data's own timestamps rather than real-world seconds.
- **Enrichment Joins**: Never call a live REST API (`GET /users/{id}`) inside a `map()` function during replay—the user's address today may differ from 30 days ago. Instead, ingest a CDC stream (`Debezium` -> Kafka) and use a Flink **Temporal Table Join** (`FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`).

## Lambda vs. Kappa vs. Lakehouse-streaming

| Dimension | Lambda Architecture | Kappa (Stream-Only) | Hybrid (Kafka + Iceberg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Codebases** | 2 (Batch + Speed) | 1 (Stream only) | 1–2 (Unified SQL / Flink) |
| **Historical Backfill** | Nightly/ad-hoc Spark job | Parallel stream job from offset 0 | Flink batch-mode read over Iceberg |
| **Storage Medium** | HDFS/Parquet + Kafka | Kafka Tiered Storage (S3/GCS) | Kafka (hot) + Iceberg/Parquet (cold) |
| **Complex Joins / ML** | Strong (Spark SQL) | Harder (large RocksDB state) | Strong (time-travel SQL + stream) |
| **Operational Overhead** | High (dual pipelines + reconciliation) | Moderate (Flink + Tiered Kafka) | Moderate-High (catalog + compaction) |

## Failure modes

- **Schema evolution breakage**: Replaying 6-month-old Avro/Protobuf events crashes `v2` if a non-nullable field was added recently without backward-compatible defaults. Enforce `BACKWARD` or `FULL` compatibility in Schema Registry.
- **Kafka partition-count rigidity**: Changing a topic from 12 to 48 partitions breaks key-based ordering for existing keys unless you migrate to a new topic (`orders-v2`) during a controlled cutover.
- **Unbounded RocksDB checkpoint bloat**: Forgetting `StateTtlConfig` on session or deduplication state causes checkpoint sizes to grow linearly forever.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Scaling Kappa with Tiered Storage and Iceberg
sections.content:
## Scaling Kappa with Tiered Storage and Iceberg

Pure Kafka broker disks become cost-prohibitive beyond 7–30 days of high-volume events. Modern Kappa deployments solve this with **Kafka Tiered Storage** (KIP-405 / Confluent / Redpanda), which asynchronously ships closed log segments to S3/GCS while keeping hot tail segments in broker page cache. For teams that also need ad-hoc SQL or ML training, **Apache Iceberg** (or Paimon/Hudi) acts as a complementary lakehouse sink: Flink reads historical Iceberg snapshots in bounded batch mode and seamlessly switches to the live Kafka stream (Flink Hybrid Source) for zero-duplicate cutover.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use event-time timestamps and bounded-out-of-orderness watermarks with `withIdleness` on every stream job.
- [ ] Enforce `BACKWARD` or `FULL` schema compatibility in Schema Registry so historical replays never fail deserialization.
- [ ] Enable Kafka Tiered Storage (or compacted topics for entity state) sized to your maximum regulatory/bug-fix replay horizon.
- [ ] Isolate all replays into parallel `v2` tables/indices and perform atomic alias/view swaps only after lag reaches zero.
- [ ] Replace synchronous external API calls in stream operators with CDC streams and temporal joins.

interviewProblems.title: Kappa Stream-Only Architecture
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Kappa Stream-Only Architecture. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Kappa architecture eliminates the separate batch layer of Lambda architecture by treating an append-only distributed log as the single source of truth for both real-time processing and historical replay.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Replay Job v2 applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Serving Store.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Serving Store experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Write replay output to an isolated staging table/index (`view_v2`), throttle sink writes, or bulk-load SSTables/Iceberg files before swapping.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: One code path, one immutable log: when business logic changes, you spin up a second stream job from offset 0, backfill a new serving table, and atomically swap pointers.
Avoid trap: Replaying directly into the live production table (`UPSERT` in place), corrupting active views with mixed v1 and v2 aggregations.
Avoid trap: Using processing time (`System.currentTimeMillis()`) instead of event time, which collapses 30 days of historical events into a single 10-minute window during replay.
When to reach for it: Real-time analytics, fraud scoring, CDC materialized views, and feature stores where maintaining dual batch/stream codebases causes drift.
When to reach for it: Event-sourced domains where retaining days, months, or infinite history in Kafka Tiered Storage (S3/GCS) or Apache Pulsar is practical.

putItTogether.title: Putting Kappa Stream Only Together
putItTogether.summary: One code path, one immutable log: when business logic changes, you spin up a second stream job from offset 0, backfill a new serving table, and atomically swap pointers.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Kappa Stream Only before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Engineers deploy `surge-v2` with a new consumer group starting at the 14-day-ago Kafka offset in Tiered Storage. Flink processes 14 days of events at 400k events/sec into a fresh OpenSearch index `surge_v2`, catches up to real-time in 45 minutes, and flips the `surge_live` alias atomically.
